name: Fizzing Volcano
hint: Two things from the kitchen cupboard. One is sour.
fact: The acid in vinegar swaps partners with baking soda and releases carbon dioxide. The mixture actually gets colder as it fizzes.

name: Sodium Meets Water
hint: A soft metal kept under oil, and the most ordinary liquid there is.
fact: Sodium tears water apart, releasing hydrogen and so much heat that the metal melts into a racing silver ball. What is left in the water is caustic sodium hydroxide.

name: Lilac Fire
hint: Sodium's bigger, angrier cousin, and water.
fact: Potassium reacts so fast that the hydrogen ignites at once. The lilac colour comes from potassium atoms in the flame.

name: The Patient Alkali
hint: The lightest metal, in water.
fact: Lithium releases more energy per atom than sodium, but it reacts slowly and does not melt, so it just fizzes steadily.

name: Milky Water
hint: A hard grey metal from the same family as magnesium, in water.
fact: Calcium bubbles hydrogen and leaves calcium hydroxide, which barely dissolves and turns the water cloudy.

name: Gentle Sodium
hint: Sodium again, but in something you could set on fire.
fact: Alcohols react with sodium the same way water does, only calmly. Chemists use this to destroy leftover sodium safely.

name: Elephant Toothpaste
hint: A pharmacy bottle, something from the bakery, and a squirt of dish soap.
fact: Yeast contains catalase, an enzyme that splits peroxide into water and oxygen. Dish soap traps the oxygen in bubbles, so it climbs out of the container like toothpaste.

name: Neutralisation
hint: An acid and a base cancel out.
fact: Acid plus base gives salt plus water, and always gives off heat.

name: Metal Eats Acid
hint: A reactive metal ribbon in something sour.
fact: Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series push hydrogen out of acids. Copper and gold cannot.

name: Rising Agent
hint: Heat the white powder that makes cakes rise.
fact: Above about 100 C baking soda breaks down and releases carbon dioxide and steam, leaving washing soda behind.

name: Caramel
hint: Heat something sweet, gently.
fact: Caramelisation is sugar breaking down by heat alone. No other ingredient is involved.

name: Burnt Offering
hint: Keep heating the caramel.
fact: Strip the water out of sugar and what remains is nearly pure carbon.

name: White Fire
hint: A silvery ribbon held in a flame until it catches.
fact: Magnesium burns at about 3000 C with a light so bright it was used for early flash photography. It keeps burning in carbon dioxide and steam, so water makes it worse.

name: Flash Powder
hint: A kitchen metal will burn, but only as a fine powder and only when very hot.
fact: A lump of aluminium is protected by its oxide skin. Fine powder has so much surface that it burns in a flash.

name: Iron Sulfide
hint: Grey filings and yellow powder, mixed and heated hard.
fact: Once it starts, the reaction makes its own heat and a red glow creeps through the mixture.

name: Glowing Charcoal
hint: The black element, and a flame.
fact: Charcoal burns without much flame because it is nearly pure carbon with nothing to vaporise.

name: Blue Flame
hint: Burn the yellow powder.
fact: Sulfur burns with a ghostly blue flame and makes sulfur dioxide, the choking gas from struck matches.

name: White Smoke
hint: A dark red powder, heated past 260 C.
fact: Burning phosphorus makes a dense white smoke of phosphorus pentoxide. Military smoke screens work the same way.

name: Spirit Flame
hint: A clear liquid that is not water, and a spark.
fact: Ethanol burns cleanly to carbon dioxide and water. The pale blue flame is almost invisible in bright light.

name: Black Copper
hint: Heat the orange metal in air.
fact: The black coat on heated copper is copper oxide. Hot hydrogen can turn it back into shiny metal.

name: Rust
hint: Grey filings, water, air and patience. Salt helps.
fact: Rusting is slow burning. The same reaction that takes years on a bridge powers disposable hand warmers.

name: Squeaky Pop
hint: Collect the gas from a fizzing metal and bring a flame.
fact: Hydrogen and oxygen make water with a bang. A small sample gives the squeaky pop every chemistry student knows.

name: Oil Floats on Water
hint: Two liquids that refuse to mix.
fact: Oil is about 8% less dense than water, and water molecules prefer each other's company.

name: Dissolving
hint: Stir a white crystal into water.
fact: The solid has not vanished. Its particles are spread out among the water molecules, and the mass is all still there.

name: Saturated Solution
hint: Keep adding until no more will dissolve.
fact: Every solid has a limit. For salt it is about 36 g per 100 mL of water.

name: Oobleck
hint: About two parts cornstarch to one part water.
fact: Oobleck is a shear-thickening fluid. Move slowly and it flows; hit it and it locks solid.

name: Red Means Acid
hint: Add indicator to something sour.
fact: Acids have a pH below 7. Vinegar is about pH 2.4.

name: Purple Means Alkali
hint: Add indicator to what sodium leaves behind in water.
fact: Strong bases push the pH toward 14. Sodium hydroxide solution is caustic enough to dissolve hair.

name: Green Means Neutral
hint: Add indicator to plain water.
fact: Pure water sits at pH 7, exactly between acid and base.

name: Boiling Point
hint: Heat water and watch the thermometer stop climbing.
fact: Boiling water stays at 100 C however hard you heat it. The extra energy goes into making steam.

name: Crystals from Brine
hint: Boil salt water until it is dry.
fact: Evaporating the water leaves the dissolved salt behind. This is how sea salt is made.

name: Melting Point
hint: Heat a solid until it gives up.
fact: Every pure substance melts at its own fixed temperature, which is one way chemists identify it.

name: Red Hot
hint: Heat a piece of metal until it glows.
fact: Everything glows the same colour at the same temperature: dull red near 550 C, orange near 900 C, white above 1300 C.

name: Sink or Float
hint: Drop a solid into a liquid.
fact: An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid. Lithium floats on oil; gold sinks in everything.

name: Iron Floats
hint: There is one liquid on the shelf that iron floats on.
fact: Mercury is 13.5 times denser than water. Iron, copper and even lead float on it.

name: Nothing Happens
hint: Try the yellow metal in anything at all.
fact: Gold is so unreactive that it is found in nature as pure metal.

name: Many Smaller Glasses
hint: Glassware and gravity.
fact: Glass breaks when an impact puts more energy into it than its surface cracks can absorb.

name: First Explosion
hint: Too much of a good thing, plus a spark.
fact: An explosion is just a fast reaction that makes hot gas faster than it can get out of the way.

name: Unstable Mystery Mixture
hint: Mix five or more things that have no business together.
fact: Real chemists call this 'the waste beaker'.

name: Strong Acid Meets Strong Base
hint: The 1 M acid and the 1 M alkali from the teaching cabinet, in equal amounts.
fact: Hydrochloric acid gives H+ ions and sodium hydroxide gives OH- ions. They join to make water, and what is left over is table salt dissolved in it. This always releases heat: about 57 kJ for every mole of water made.

name: Acid Fizz
hint: Hydrochloric acid on something from the kitchen that makes cakes rise.
fact: Any acid plus a carbonate or bicarbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. A strong acid fizzes much faster than vinegar because it has far more H+ ions at the same strength.

name: Marble Dissolves
hint: Hydrochloric acid and a piece of stone used for statues.
fact: Calcium carbonate reacts with acid to make calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide. Acid rain slowly does the same to marble buildings and limestone cliffs.

name: Iron in Acid
hint: Iron nails or filings in hydrochloric acid. Be patient.
fact: Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it pushes hydrogen out of the acid. It is slower than magnesium because iron is less reactive. The solution turns pale green from iron(II) chloride.

name: Black Powder, Blue-Green Liquid
hint: Heat copper until it turns black, then put the black stuff in hydrochloric acid. Warmth helps.
fact: Metal oxides are bases: they neutralise acids to make a salt and water. Copper oxide dissolves to give blue-green copper chloride. No gas is made, because there is no metal to push hydrogen out.

name: Sherbet Fizz
hint: The sour crystals and the cake-rising powder, with a little water.
fact: Citric acid and baking soda do nothing while dry, but in water they react to release carbon dioxide. That is how sherbet and bath bombs fizz. The reaction takes in heat, which is why sherbet feels cool on your tongue.

name: Copper Plating a Nail
hint: Drop iron or magnesium into blue copper sulfate solution.
fact: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound. Iron is more reactive than copper, so pink-brown copper coats the iron and the blue colour fades to pale green as iron sulfate forms.

name: Blue Crystals Turn White
hint: Heat blue copper sulfate crystals in a crucible.
fact: The blue colour comes from water molecules held inside the crystal. Heat drives that water off as steam and leaves white anhydrous copper sulfate. This is a reversible reaction.

name: The Test for Water
hint: Add a few drops of water to the white powder you made by heating copper sulfate.
fact: White anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue the moment water touches it, and warms up as it does. Chemists use it to test whether a liquid contains water.

name: Crystals on Cooling
hint: Dissolve as much copper sulfate or alum as you can in hot water, then cool it down.
fact: Hot water can hold far more dissolved solid than cold water. As a saturated hot solution cools, the extra solid has nowhere to go and comes out as crystals. Cooling slowly gives fewer, bigger crystals.

name: Pink Means Alkali
hint: A few drops of phenolphthalein in an alkali.
fact: Phenolphthalein stays colourless in acids and neutral water, then turns bright pink above about pH 8.2. Because the change is so sharp, it is used to spot the exact end of a titration.

name: Cabbage Rainbow
hint: Red cabbage juice in something strongly acidic, and in something strongly alkaline.
fact: Red cabbage juice is a natural indicator. Its anthocyanin dye changes shape as the pH changes, and each shape absorbs a different colour of light: red in strong acid, purple at neutral, green and then yellow in strong alkali.

name: The Endpoint
hint: Watch an indicator while you add alkali to an acid, a little at a time.
fact: The moment the indicator changes colour is the endpoint: just enough alkali has been added to cancel the acid. Measuring how much it took is called a titration, and it tells you how strong the acid was.

name: Campfire
hint: Something from under the trees, held in a flame.
fact: Burning wood combines its carbon and hydrogen with oxygen from the air, making carbon dioxide and water and releasing heat and light.

name: Green Rock Turns Black
hint: Heat the green rock from the forest.
fact: Malachite breaks down when heated, giving off carbon dioxide and steam and leaving black copper oxide. It is the first step in getting copper out of rock.

name: Copper from Rock
hint: The black powder from roasted green rock, mixed with charcoal powder and heated very hard.
fact: Carbon pulls oxygen away from copper oxide, leaving copper metal. This is smelting, the discovery that started the Bronze Age.

name: Iron from Rock
hint: Crushed red rock and charcoal powder, hotter than copper needs.
fact: Iron ore is iron oxide. Carbon takes its oxygen at around 1000 C. It needs far more heat than copper, which is why the Iron Age came after the Bronze Age.

name: Burning Lime
hint: Heat a piece of limestone until it glows white.
fact: Limestone (calcium carbonate) gives off carbon dioxide above about 840 C and turns into quicklime. Lime kilns have done this for thousands of years.

name: Slaking Lime
hint: Add water to quicklime.
fact: Quicklime reacts with water so violently that it hisses and steams. The product, slaked lime, is used in mortar and to make limewater.

name: Making Glass
hint: Sand, plus what baking soda becomes when you heat it, melted together.
fact: Sand alone melts at about 1700 C. Adding soda (sodium carbonate) brings that down so it can be melted in an ordinary furnace. This is how glass has been made for 3500 years.

name: Berry Indicator
hint: Crushed dark berries in water, then something sour or something soapy.
fact: Elderberries hold anthocyanins, the same dyes as red cabbage. Their juice turns red in acid and green-blue in alkali, so people could test acids and alkalis long before lab indicators existed.

name: Crystal on a String
hint: Hang a crystal thread in a hot, saturated solution and let it cool.
fact: Crystals need somewhere to start. A rough thread gives the dissolved ions a place to line up, so one big crystal grows there instead of many tiny ones on the bottom. Rock candy is grown the same way from sugar.
